title: Present value honestly and invite challenge
nav: 4. Present value honestly and invite challenge
objective: Respond when the CFO says 'these are estimates, not savings'.
clearance: Rewritten draft; pending SME and partner clearance

blocks.x: Executives trust a value case they can challenge. Present ranges, label evidence, and let the customer's own people speak to their experience.
Link DITL evidence to cost, risk, or revenue. Show:

items: **The value range:** conservative, base, and upside.
**The material assumptions**, with their evidence level.
**The plan to verify:** metric owners, baselines, and timing.

blocks.x: Let the champion or workflow owners confirm their experience in their own words. Don't speak for them.
State plainly that modeled capacity benefit is not confirmed P&L savings. Then ask:

items: "What outcome would justify the investment for you?"

blocks.x: The answers become the success criteria.

blocks.label: Boundary
blocks.x: Don't make the optimistic scenario the headline without its caveats. Don't present internal benchmarks that aren't cleared for external use as independent proof.
Anchor on the customer's own numbers

Glean's business-case training recommends presenting multiple ROI scenarios anchored in company-specific data. When an executive challenges an estimate, the strongest response is to show where each input came from and which assumption matters most, then agree how it will be checked. Glean's value-selling training adds that cost reduction is easier to quantify while growth drivers tend to have stronger executive impact, so be clear which numbers are which.

blocks.title: Answering an executive challenge
blocks.alt: A comparison of weak and strong responses when an executive challenges a value estimate. A weak response defends the number or cites a benchmark. A strong response shows the input sources, names the key assumption, and agrees how it will be measured.
